The session begins.

The Basilisk Gate is behind you, and the city closes around you the way big ports do: noise, lamplight, too many people with somewhere to be. The Copper Lantern is the first door that promised warmth, and it keeps its promise. Heat from the hearth, the roar of a full taproom, the smell of fried fish and wet wool. A broad woman behind the bar is chalking names onto a slate of rooms while she pours. A young tiefling with a tray slides between benches, and more than one drinker leans away from her as she passes. In the far corner, under a swinging lantern, cards snap onto felt. The dealer has quick hands and an easy smile, and the players are hunched over their hands with the stillness of people who have money on the table. One seat there is empty. In front of it sits a small, tidy tower of coins that nobody reaches for and nobody seems to notice. The cat has stopped dead at your boots. Tail low, it stares at that empty chair and will not look away. The innkeeper glances up from her slate and catches your eye across the room. She raises her brows: a bed, a drink, or just the door letting in the cold?

Your hand finds the cloak's edge instead of the card case. The cat ignores your mutter. It pads after you to the bar, then sits down sideways across your boots, between you and the corner, and goes back to staring.

The innkeeper finishes her chalk line before she looks up. Up close she smells of flour and lye. Her forearms could knead a man as easily as dough.

"Worgen." She writes it on the slate in big square letters, under a smudge that used to be somebody else. "Bed's at the top of the stair, second on the left. Five silver. Supper's fish or stew, and with a mug that's nine silver altogether. I'll take it when you've eaten, not before. Nobody ever paid me for a meal they hated." She lifts a mug from under the bar and pulls the ale without looking at the tap. It's brown and cold, with a head that holds.

When you ask about the chair, her hand stops on the tap for half a breath.

"Nobody's." She says it loud, the way she says everything, but it's meant for you. "Nobody sits there, nobody clears it, and nobody touches that pile. House rule, and it's my house." She sets the mug in front of you and leans on her knuckles. "Last winter a dockhand thought he'd be clever. He reached for it, then stood there with his hand out like he'd walked into a room and forgotten why. Couldn't tell my girl his own name till she'd poured him a second. He hasn't been back." Her eyes drop to the cat, then come back up. "Your cat's got more sense than he had."

Behind you the tiefling server slips past with an empty tray. Her eyes go to the corner and away, quick as a flinch. Her face shows nothing.

At the card table the dealer has noticed the new face at the bar. He gives you an easy, open smile, the kind that costs nothing, and lifts two fingers off the deck. "Plenty of room, friend, when you've had your supper." He never once looks at the chair beside him, with its little tower of coins.

Hesta raps the bar once to get your attention back.

"So. Fish or stew?"

At the card table, Dorrin laughs at your answer. It's a short, easy laugh, and two of his players look up from their hands to see what's funny.

"Retired! Friend, I've met that creditor. Everyone in this room owes her something." He squares the deck with one tap and starts dealing again without looking at his hands. "Offer doesn't spoil. The chair's warm whenever you like." He means the chair across from him, by the wall. His eyes slide past the other one the way water runs around a stone.

When you lower your voice, Hesta leans in on her elbows, close enough that the noise of the room covers her.

"Warn them?" She snorts through her nose. "He doesn't need to. Watch for a night. Folk walk around that chair like it's a puddle. Drunks, sailors, the Fist when they come in for their free mug. Him too." She jerks her chin at the corner. "He came with the table five winters back, near enough. Pays his corner rent on time, never starts a fight, never lets one start. I've had worse dealers." She pauses, then adds flatly: "I've had better company."

She straightens up and raises her voice again for the room. "Ilsa! Fish, and a plain piece with no sauce for the gentleman's cat."

A few minutes later the tiefling girl comes back through the crowd with your supper on a board. There's fried fish with the crust still crackling, a heel of dark bread and a spoon of something green and sharp on the side. On a chipped saucer is a skinned piece of fish with nothing on it at all. She sets your plate on the bar. Then she crouches and puts the saucer on the floor by your boots, careful to keep her tail clear of the drinkers' feet.

The cat doesn't eat. It hasn't moved, and its eyes are still fixed on the corner.

Ilsa stays crouched a moment longer than she needs to and watches the cat watch. Her own eyes go to the corner and come back. When she stands, her face is blank again and polite.

"If he doesn't want it, sir, just leave the saucer. I'll take it when I clear." She's already half turned toward the next table.

"You're welcome, sir." Ilsa gives a quick, polite dip of the head and turns away with her tray. Two benches on she looks back once. She sees you down on the boards beside the cat, then she's gone into the crowd.

The cat's fur is warm under your hand and stiff along the spine, not quite raised. It doesn't lean into you the way it usually does. It doesn't move away either.

Your question goes down the bond, and the answer comes back the way the cat's answers always do. There are no words, only things felt.

First comes **cold**. It isn't the cold of a draught or a winter doorstep. It's the cold of a hearth that has been out a long time, in a room where somebody still sits waiting. With it comes a sense of **small**. Whatever the cat is looking at isn't up at a man's height. It's lower, about the height of the chair's seat back. If you didn't know there was nothing there, you would think of a child.

The third thing is stranger, and it makes the hair on your own arms prickle. It's **familiar**. The cat gives you a scent, or something like one: the faint brightness that clings to the worn coin in your pocket, the warmth that sometimes comes when you call on the Lady's light. Here that same warmth has been stretched thin and gone cold at the edges, like a coat worn too long by someone with no fire.

The coins don't come into it at all. To the cat they are only metal. The chair is wood. What it is watching is the *someone*.

Last comes a feeling that isn't about the corner at all. The cat shifts its weight and presses its flank against your shins, firm and deliberate. It's planted between your knees and the card table. The meaning reaches you as plainly as a hand on your chest: *not you. Don't you sit there.*

Over your head the taproom goes on roaring. At the corner table cards snap down, someone groans, and coins slide across the felt towards Dorrin. Beside him the little tower stays where it is. The lantern above it swings gently, and nobody looks at it.

The fish on the saucer has stopped steaming.

The cat's answer comes back down the bond: *good*. Its spine loosens a little under your hand, not all the way. It stays where it is, across your boots, and keeps watching the chair.

You stand up. Hesta has moved off to pull two mugs for a pair of carters, and she comes back along the bar wiping her hands on her apron. When she hears your question she leans in again on her elbows, close enough to keep it between the two of you.

"A child?" She shakes her head. "No children in my house after dark. That's not a rule, it's sense. This is a dock tavern."

She starts to straighten up, then stops halfway. The rag in her hand goes still.

"There was a little fellow. Not a child. A halfling, grown, with grey in his whiskers. He had a room upstairs for a season." She frowns, like someone feeling for a step in the dark. "He paid me in jokes more than in silver. Good jokes, mind you. He owed me three months by the end."

The frown deepens.

"I chalked his name on that slate every week. Every week, and I..." She glances at the slate behind her and its rows of smudges. Her jaw tightens. "I can't call it up. I remember the jokes. I don't remember his name."

She says it flatly, but she doesn't like it. You can see that in how hard she wipes a spot on the bar that's already clean.

"A coin, now." She snorts quietly. "He flipped one for everything. Fish or stew. Rain or no rain. Whether he'd pay me this week. Always the same one, an old gold piece, worn smooth. I never looked at whose face was on it." For a moment her knuckles rest on the edge of the shelf under the bar, then come away again. "Then one morning he was gone. His bed hadn't been slept in. And that corner's been cold ever since. I'm not saying those two things are the same thing. I'm saying that's when."

She straightens up properly and looks at you. It's a long, plain look, the look of a woman who has had travellers lie to her across this bar for thirty years.

"Now you tell me something. Why would a man off the road ask me about the Lady's coin? You're not temple. You don't have the look." Her mouth thins. "And you'd better not be. I don't care for priests."

Hesta watches the coin come out from under your collar. She doesn't lean in to look at it. She looks at you, the same long, plain look as before, and she keeps it up after the coin is gone again.

"Soldier I'd have guessed," she says at last. "It's in how you stand. The gambler I believe even more." Her eyes go to the cat, which still sits pressed across your boots. "And I've never yet heard a priest say *I won't pretend*. They always know."

She breathes out through her nose. Then she bends down behind the bar, with a grunt for her knees, and you hear her shift crocks and a coil of rope on the shelf there. When she straightens up she has a box in both hands and sets it on the bar between your mug and your cooling supper.

It's small, about the size of a loaf. It's old, dark wood bound at the corners with iron gone brown. The lock is a plain iron plate with a keyhole, and the wood around the hole is scratched pale, as if someone tried it with a knife once and thought better of it. A paper tag hangs from one corner on a loop of string. The writing on it is big and square, the same hand as the slate.

**KEPT FOR**

The paper after those two words is bare. There's no smudge and no scratch-out. The ink of *KEPT FOR* is as black as the day it was written. After it there's only a clean space, about one short name wide, where the paper has gone slightly smoother than the rest, the way a coin's face wears smooth.

Hesta sees you looking at the tag. Her mouth sets.

"I wrote his name on that. I *know* I did." She doesn't touch the tag. "Found this under his bed the morning he was gone. Kept it against the three months. Never opened it. It's not mine to open, and I never had the key. Somebody had a go with a blade one night, mind you. That wasn't me either." She rests a broad hand flat on the lid, not quite letting go. "I've had it under there five winters. Every time I think of selling it, I don't."

Over at the corner table cards slap down and a man swears cheerfully. Dorrin's laugh rises easily over it. Nobody is looking this way. You notice that Hesta has checked that before she says anything more.

"So, here's how it goes." She keeps her voice down. "If you open it, you open it here, at my bar, where I can see. And if there's silver inside, my three months come out first. He'd have wanted that. He joked about it often enough." Her hand stays on the lid. "Agreed?"

At your feet the cat has turned its head away from the corner for the first time tonight. It's looking up at the box.

Hesta's hand stays flat on the lid a moment longer, then lifts.

"At his rate." She nods once, short. "That's fair. He had the little room under the eaves, and he was little, so it was a little rate. I know the sum to the copper. I wrote it on that slate twelve weeks running." She steps back half a pace from the box, the way you'd step back from a horse you weren't sure of. "And the rest stays his. Good. I'd have said the same if you hadn't."

You leave the lock alone. You turn the box under the lantern light without lifting it far off the bar. The wood is old and dense, oak or something like it, dark from years of hands and smoke. The iron corners have rusted brown but they're sound. The knife marks round the keyhole are shallow and impatient, made by someone who gave up quickly. On the underside, in the corner where a thumb would rest when you carried it, someone has cut a tiny mark into the grain with a knife point: a circle the size of a fingernail, with a short notch in its rim, the way you'd nick a coin to know it again.

Then you turn to the tag. You don't scrape it and you don't wet it. You tilt it to the light and look at the blank where the name should be. At the same time you reach for the warmth the pact keeps in you, the small sense of things that aren't only wood and paper, and you let yourself feel for whatever touched it.

"Under the bar it is, then," Hesta says. She slides the box off the counter and down out of sight in one practised movement, and you hear it settle back among the crocks and rope. She doesn't argue.

You take your mug and cross the room. The crowd parts for you without trying, the way it parts for that corner. You stop a few feet short of the empty chair and stand where the players can still see their cards past your elbow. Up close it's a plain chair, the same as all the others, with the seat polished by years of nobody. The little tower of coins sits on the felt in front of it. The lantern swings slowly above it.

You talk low, under the noise of the room, into the space at seat-back height where the cat was looking.

"Hesta's kept your box. The one with the nicked-coin mark, so your luck could find its way home." A breath. "James Worgen. Can you hear me?"

Nothing happens at first. A carter at the table tosses in a coin and asks for a card. Dorrin deals.

Then the coin under your collar goes cold. It isn't a chill. It's the sudden deep cold of metal left out on a winter windowsill, cold enough that your skin flinches from it. When you breathe out, your breath fogs. It's only one faint grey puff in a hot, crowded taproom by the hearth, and it's gone before it reaches the lantern.

The answer comes down the bond, from the cat at the bar behind you. It doesn't come in the cat's own way. The feelings come thinner and stranger, like a voice carried in from another room. First comes **surprise**, sharp and almost painful, like someone woken by his own name and finding it isn't his. Then comes something that would be a laugh if it had any breath in it. Then comes **you came**, and under it, fainter, **she sent you**. With it comes a pull, a small tug like a hand on your sleeve, back towards the bar and the box beneath it.

Then the cat's own feeling cuts across all of that, flat and firm: *close enough. No closer.*

On the polished edge of the table, in front of the empty chair, a thin rime of frost spreads across the wood. It's no wider than a thumbnail. It makes a circle with a short notch in the rim. It holds for the space of a heartbeat, then it beads into water and is only a damp mark that anyone would take for spilled ale.

Dorrin's hands stop.

It lasts no longer than the frost did. The card he was sliding to the carter turns over halfway and lands face up on the felt, the six of cups. One of the players says "Hey, now," and another laughs. Dorrin laughs with them, quick and easy, and sweeps the card back into the deck.

"Misdeal. My fault, my round, drinks on the house." He shuffles again without looking down. His eyes come up to you. He doesn't look at the chair, or the damp mark, or the coins. They come straight to your face and stay there, still friendly, and very attentive.

"Talking to the lantern, friend?" He smiles. "It's a terrible listener. The seat by the wall's a better one." He taps the deck once against the felt. "You sure that creditor of yours isn't open to terms?"

Dorrin's smile stays put when you say you'll stay on her good side. His eyes go to the mug in your hand, then to the wall seat you haven't taken, and he lets both go with a little shrug.

"Her good side." He cuts the deck one-handed and closes it again. "Wise. I hear it's a narrow one."

Then you ask about the halfling. He doesn't answer straight away. He deals the next round first, one card to each player, snap, snap, snap, and skips the chair beside him so smoothly you'd only notice if you were counting. The carter with the face-up six pulls his new card in close to his chest.

"Five winters," he says. "In a dock tavern, that's a lot of whiskers through the door. Halflings off the river barges, halflings off the Amn caravans. Grey ones, brown ones, one with a beard down to his belt buckle who swore he was a dwarf." The players laugh. Dorrin laughs too. "Good jokes, you said? Then he wasn't one of mine. Never sat at my table, that one. Not once."

Most men wouldn't have heard anything odd in that. You've spent half your life across a table from men like him, and you hear it. You didn't ask whether the halfling played. Dorrin answered that question anyway, quickly, before you could ask it. While he spoke, his thumb ran along the edge of the deck, back and forth, the way a man's hand goes to a sore tooth.

There's something else, and it's harder to place. When he got to *what did you call him*, he started to answer. His mouth began to shape something, and then a frown went across his face. It was the same frown Hesta had at the bar, the look of a man reaching for a stair that isn't there. It lasted half a breath before he smiled it away. He's hiding something about that halfling. But there's at least one thing he truly can't find, and the name is it.

"Tell you what." He leans back and spreads his hands over the felt. "My memory's better with something to do. Sit one hand, no stake, just keep me company, and maybe it comes back to me." He nods at the wall seat. "No money on the table. Your creditor can't object to that, can she?"

**No. 4471**

*To the next one she sends.*

*If you're reading this, two things are true. She sent you, and I lost. I'm sorry about the second one. I did try.*

*My name is*

*There, I expect you've noticed something wrong with that line. If I've guessed right about what they do to a man, you can't read it and the good woman downstairs can't remember it. Tell her the jokes were free and the rent wasn't, and I know it.*

A patriar on the hill, Lord Esmond Ardanne, has been buying fair winds for his ships, and he isn't buying them from Umberlee. There's a paper. I've seen the bottom of it. *I couldn't get at the paper, so he offered me a way. One game at a table of his choosing, me against his luck. If I win, the paper burns. If I lose, I'm staked. He was very polite about what that means. The dealer is a sharp called Vasque. He isn't a good one, and that's the only reason I said yes.*

*Then a clerk with black under his nails took my coin, her coin, the one the Hall gave me, and scraped her face off the back of it to seal the wager. It won't land since then. Not heads, not tails. It stands up on its edge and looks at me. I've flipped it a hundred times tonight.*

*So I've put it where neither they nor I can easily get at it. The ticket's in with this. If I win, I'll fetch it back myself for a silver and you'll never read a word of this. If you are reading it, go and get it before they think to. And don't throw it until you know which side you want it to land on. I don't know. That's the truth, and it's why I haven't thrown it.*

*Three things, and then I'll stop being serious, because it doesn't suit me.*

*Don't sit in any chair at a table they're running.*

*Don't touch whatever's piled in front of it, however it looks.*

*Don't let anybody wager you. Not for you, not against you, not even as a joke.*

*I told the Hall. The Hall told me to be patient. Don't go to them first.*

*Good luck. I mean that professionally.*

There's a dash at the bottom, and after it the same smooth nothing your eyes won't hold. Under that, drawn by hand in the ink, is the circle with the notch in its rim.

Ilsa doesn't say anything. As you go she gives you a small nod, the kind a server gives a regular, and then the kitchen hatch bangs and she's gone into the smell of porridge.

Cable Street wakes up around you as you go downhill. The cobbles are wet from a night's drizzle and shine grey in the dawn. Marl Tenby's shutters are open now, and through the window you can see him bent over a workbench with the jeweller's glass already back in his eye. He doesn't look up. Past his shop the ropewalk runs a long way under a lean-to roof. Two men walk backwards down it, twisting hemp, with the slow care of people who have done the same thing for twenty years. The air smells of tar and wet rope, and by the bottom of the street it smells of fish as well.

The fish market sprawls along the harbour wall, under a sky full of gulls. The boats came in an hour ago. Long trestle tables run in rows, and women in leather aprons stand at them gutting with short knives, so fast their hands blur. Scales fly. The gulls fight over the slops in the gutters, and one of them makes a pass at the cat. The cat turns its head and looks at it, and the gull decides it wanted something else.

At the end of the row a crier stands on an upturned crate with a bundle of broadsheets under his arm. He calls in the flat, practised bawl of a man who has been doing it since the bells.

"*Baldur's Mouth*, one copper! Fist says the Outer City curfew stands another tenday! Grain barge aground at Wyrm's Crossing! Another one in the water off the Grey Harbour steps last night, coin in his teeth like the others, and the Fist says *no foul play*! One copper, *Baldur's Mouth*!"

The nearest fishwife stops gutting just long enough to touch two wet fingers to her lips and then to the table's edge. It's a sailor's sign for Umberlee, done without thinking. Her neighbour doesn't make the sign. She spits in the gutter instead and goes back to her knife.

Behind the last row of tables, where the market backs onto an old warehouse wall, is the arch. It's a low curve of soot-black brick, older than the warehouse it's built into, and its keystone has been worn shapeless by weather. Two lads are sluicing out the market with buckets and a long-handled broom, and the dirty water runs over the cobbles straight under the arch and down. You hear it before you see the stair. It gurgles and slaps, a long way down, like water going into a well.

The steps go down steep and narrow into the dark, slick with fish slime and green weed. The first dozen are lit grey by the morning. After that there's nothing.

On the top step, with his back against the brick and out of the stream of water, sits a boy of ten or eleven. He has a shuttered tin lamp between his bare feet and a cap pulled down to his eyebrows. His feet are filthy. His eyes are sharp. He has seen your boots, your cloak and the way you carry yourself before you're halfway across the cobbles, and by the time you reach the arch he's on his feet with the lamp in one hand and the other held out, palm up.

"Copper for the light, mister." He says it the way the crier says *one copper*, like a fixed price. His eyes drop to the cat at your heel and come back up. "Cat goes free. Cats see in the dark."

Down below, the water goes on slapping at something you can't see.

My fingers stray toward the card case. I catch myself and draw my cloak closed instead.

“Not looking,” I mutter to the cat, while looking.

I approach the bar. “A bed, supper, and an ale. James Worgen.” With a small nod toward the empty chair, I lower my voice. “And whose place am I to avoid? Someone’s left their stake, and my cat seems to think they’ll want it back.”

“Fish. A little unseasoned for my sensible friend, if you can.”

I lift my mug toward the dealer without leaving the bar. “Kind of you, but I’ve retired. My last creditor was very firm about it.”

Turning back to Hesta, I keep my voice low. “I’ll respect your rule. Does the dealer warn newcomers before they sit there?”

“Thank you, Ilsa.”

I crouch beside the cat, resting a hand near its shoulders without trying to turn it away. Through our telepathic bond, I ask, *What’s troubling you? The coins, the chair, or something sitting in it?*

*I won’t sit there. Promise.*

I give the cat a gentle stroke and straighten, leaving my supper untouched for the moment.

“Hesta,” I ask quietly, “before Dorrin came, did a child have anything to do with that corner? Perhaps someone who carried a coin of the Lady’s?”

“No priest. Soldier once. Gambler after—that went worse.”

I draw my worn coin just clear of my collar, keeping it screened from the room.

“The Lady helped me when I asked. Now I owe her service, and no more cards. That was the creditor I meant.”

I tuck it away. “My cat senses someone in that chair. Small, cold, and something about them reminds him of this coin. I don’t know who it is, or what happened. I won’t pretend otherwise.”

My eyes follow her hand toward the shelf. “Did your lodger leave anything behind?”

“Agreed—your three months at the rate he owed. Anything else stays his until we know what became of him.”

I leave the lock alone for now and examine the box and tag without forcing or scraping anything, looking for symbols or signs of magic I might recognise—especially whatever has taken the name off the paper.
[Roll the die]
[Onward]

“Now I try asking the owner. Keep it safe a little longer—I’ve no wish to break his lock.”

I take my mug and walk toward the corner, stopping a few feet from the empty chair without blocking the players. I don’t touch the coins or sit.

Keeping my voice low, I address the space the cat was watching. “Hesta’s kept your box. The one with the nicked-coin mark, so your luck could find its way home.”

“James Worgen. Can you hear me?”

“Quite sure. I intend to stay on her good side.”

I keep my mug in hand and leave the offered seat alone.

“Hesta tells me you’ve been here five winters. You might remember a halfling who lodged upstairs—grey whiskers, good jokes, flipped an old gold coin for everything. What did you call him?”

“She can. No cards, Dorrin—not even a friendly hand.”

I keep my tone pleasant. “You remember him well enough to say he never played here. That’s a start. If something else comes back to you, I’ll be at the bar.”

I return to Hesta and the cat, lowering my voice. “Someone answered. Used your lodger’s mark, and seemed to want me to look in his box. Do you know a locksmith you’d trust to open it here without damaging it?”

“First light suits. I’ll pay Marl. And thank you—warming it would be kind.”

I settle onto the stool beside the cat, keeping my voice low. “One precaution: if anyone asks about that box tonight, keep it put away and come fetch me. I’d rather lose sleep than find you’ve had trouble over it.”

Then I leave the mystery alone long enough to eat my supper.

I put a gold piece on the bar. “Keep the silver for the extra fish. My companion approves, which is rarer than you’d think.”

When Ilsa next comes within earshot, I speak quietly without holding her up. “You looked as though you had something to say earlier. If it’s about that corner, I’m willing to listen—somewhere away from the table, if you prefer.”

“That someone had finally come. It seemed to think the Lady sent me.” I keep my voice as quiet as hers. “Not words exactly—feelings, through my cat. Surprised. Hopeful, I think.”

“And I believe you about the cold. Thank you for telling me.”

I glance toward the kitchen hatch, then back to her. “One question before you go: have you heard anyone come in through that yard door, or only Dorrin leaving?”

“Goodnight, Ilsa.”

I give the cat a discreet beckon and head upstairs to my room, without another look toward Dorrin.

Once inside, I close the door and check the room’s window: where it looks out, and whether I can see the yard or its gate without making myself conspicuous.

*Much better. No sitting in strange chairs tonight.*

I leave the candle unlit and settle beside the window, far enough back that my face won’t show through the gap. My cloak stays on; the rod rests within reach.

I keep watch over the yard and listen for the gate latch, waiting to see who comes to meet Dorrin after closing.

[Roll the die]
[Onward]

*We tried,* I tell the cat. *Morning, then.*

I leave the door barred, put the rod beside the bed, and take off my armour. Before lying down, I hold Tymora’s coin for a moment.

“If you sent me for him, Lady, I’ve found him. I’ll do what I can.”

I get some sleep until Hesta knocks for the locksmith.

“Coming.”

I wash my face, buckle on my armour and gather my gear, then head downstairs with the cat.

“Master Tenby? James Worgen. Thank you for coming early.” I nod toward the box. “We’d like the lock opened without damage, if possible. What’s your fee?”

I count two gold pieces onto the bar beside Marl’s tools. “Cleanly done. Thank you.”

Then I pick up the letter. “I believe this one’s meant for me.”

I carefully break the wax seal, unfold the sheets and read.

I fold the letter and put it inside my coat.

“He says the jokes were free and the rent wasn’t. He knew he owed you.” I pause. “I believe he’s still in that chair. And I have a lead on helping him.”

Keeping my voice low, I repeat his three warnings to Hesta and Ilsa. “Please take those literally. And keep what we found from Dorrin.”

I pick up the pawn ticket. “I’ll need this to recover his coin. Hesta, what’s the safest way to Griswell’s at the foot of the Wet Stair?”

“Then I’d best go before he changes his mind. Thank you, both.”

I stow the rod and tuck the ticket securely inside my coat. *Close by me,* I tell the cat.

Following Hesta’s directions, I head down Cable Street toward the fish market and the Wet Stair, keeping my hands clear of my weapons.
“Fair enough.” I stop on the level cobbles rather than venture onto the steps. “Can you change a gold piece? If not, I’ll get change in the market. No hurry worth breaking my neck over.”

I enjoyed this session. James had room to be a person before he had a quest: refusing cards, talking to an innkeeper, worrying about his cat, paying for supper. The mystery grew naturally out of those choices.

**What worked**
- Hesta, Ilsa and the cat were the strongest parts. They had distinct personalities, and small gestures made earning their trust satisfying.
- The hook fit James unusually well. The missing name, abandoned stake and trapped servant of Tymora made this personal without forcing me to sit down and gamble.
- My refusals mattered. Dorrin tempted me, but the game let me investigate another way.
- The clues were memorable and consistent: the notched coin, erased names, cold chair and coin that wouldn’t land. The letter delivered a useful payoff.
- Failed checks stayed failed, even after a reroll. I appreciated that honesty.

**What broke**
- The rules and records weren’t fully aligned. Arcana used +2 instead of +3; the failed Perception reroll was later logged as the original result. The initial record also changed some supplied character details without explanation, including rapier proficiency, Healing Light’s limit and attunement.
- Out-of-game notes sometimes explained things nobody had disputed. One referenced “the fourth item” and a “misreading” with no visible context. That felt like internal bookkeeping leaking into the scene.
- The narration occasionally treated mood as evidence—for example, James sensing Dorrin watching his back. I’d prefer observable details or clearly labelled suspicions.

**What was missing / could improve**
- More momentum. We spent most of a session on one tavern conversation and reached the next location just as play ended. The atmosphere was good, but repeated looks, pauses, rag-wiping and cat reactions sometimes slowed it down.
- Routine logistics could be bundled. Getting change for a one-copper toll became several turns without presenting much of a meaningful choice.
- Checks required a roll request, a button press and sometimes an additional “Onward.” Resolving the narration immediately after the roll would help.
- A little more ordinary city life alongside the mystery would make the setting feel less arranged around it. The fish market and broadsheet were welcome.

Overall, I’d gladly continue. Keep the characterful NPCs and respect for player choice; tighten the repetition, streamline routine actions and make the mechanical records dependable.

Yes—during the night watch. When the visitor arrived, I wanted the option to send the cat closer to the back door to listen, or quietly move downstairs myself.

After the failed Perception roll, the narration covered his entire visit and departure. By the time I could act again, he was gone. I accepted that rather than ask to rewind, but failing to identify him from the window didn’t mean I wanted to abandon the investigation.

A pause at “you hear two voices below, but can’t make out the words” would have helped. Then I could choose whether to risk getting closer or stay safely upstairs. The failed roll would still matter without closing the whole opportunity.

**KEPT FOR**

"One more thing, and then I've got to go. When Hesta bars the door, he doesn't go home. Dorrin. He stays at that table with the lamp, and Hesta sends me up to bed before she does anything else." She picks up the stack again and holds it against her chest. "I don't know what he's waiting for. I've only heard the yard door, and it isn't Hesta."

She looks at you over the top of the boards.

"What did it say to you, sir? When you talked to it."

“That someone had finally come. It seemed to think the Lady sent me.” I keep my voice as quiet as hers. “Not words exactly—feelings, through my cat. Surprised. Hopeful, I think.”

“And I believe you about the cold. Thank you for telling me.”

I glance toward the kitchen hatch, then back to her. “One question before you go: have you heard anyone come in through that yard door, or only Dorrin leaving?”
turns.reply:
Ilsa listens without looking up from the boards. Her hands stop when you say *the Lady sent me*, then start again, squaring a stack that's already square.

"Hopeful." She says it under her breath, as though she's trying the word out. She doesn't ask which lady. Most likely she knows. In this city a man who talks about the Lady and carries himself like a soldier only means one.

When you thank her, she lifts her eyes to your face for a moment. She doesn't smile, but something in her shoulders eases.

"Nobody's said that to me before." That's all she says about it.

Your glance toward the hatch makes her glance there too. In the kitchen the pots have gone quiet. She lowers her voice even further.

"Somebody comes in. Dorrin doesn't go out, not by the yard." She speaks slowly, picking each piece out carefully. "My room's at the back, over the yard. I'm awake, mostly. First the latch on the yard gate, then boots on the stones. They aren't dock boots. They have hard heels, the kind that click, like the men from up the hill wear when they come down to the quays and don't want anyone to forget it." She pauses. "They cross to the back door, it opens, and then it's voices downstairs. Two of them, too low for words. Not long. Then the boots again, and the gate."

She hefts the boards against her chest.

"Dorrin goes out the front after, when Hesta lets him. Late. I've never seen the other one's face. I've never looked." She says that last part flatly, the way a person states a rule they live by. "Looking's how you get noticed."

"*Ilsa!*" Hesta's voice comes down the bar, loud enough to lift heads at the hearth. "Hatch is backing up, girl!"

"Coming!" She's already half turned. Then she looks back once, past her horns, at the cat loafed on the stool, and then at you.

"Goodnight, sir. Cockcrow, I'm down to Cable Street. I'll bring Marl myself."

She's gone through the crowd towards the kitchen hatch, quick and careful, her tail kept clear of the benches.

Behind you the cards fall. Dorrin laughs at something a carter said, warm and easy. The room has thinned out. A third of the benches are empty now, and the hearth has burned down to a red bed with one log on it. Under the lantern in the corner, the little tower of coins sits untouched.

The cat opens one eye, looks at the corner, and closes it again.

turns.message:
“Goodnight, Ilsa.”

I give the cat a discreet beckon and head upstairs to my room, without another look toward Dorrin.

Once inside, I close the door and check the room’s window: where it looks out, and whether I can see the yard or its gate without making myself conspicuous.
turns.reply:
"Goodnight, sir." Ilsa doesn't look up from the hatch, but she nods.

You crook two fingers low by your knee. The cat opens both eyes, stretches until its claws show, and drops off the stool without any hurry, as if it had decided to go up anyway. It follows you through the thinning crowd and up the narrow stair, one step behind your heel the whole way. You don't look at the corner. Behind you a card snaps down onto the felt, and the taproom noise falls away as the stairwell turns.

The second door on the left has a latch and a wooden bar on the inside. The room behind it is small and clean, and it smells of lye like Hesta. There's a bed under a grey wool blanket, a washstand with a cracked jug, a peg for your cloak and a stub of tallow candle in a dish. The floorboards let the noise of the bar come up through them, softened. You can hear voices, a laugh, a bench scraping. Hesta's voice carries even through a floor.

You close the door and drop the bar.

The window is a single pane of thick, bubbled glass behind a pair of wooden shutters. One shutter has a broken slat about two fingers wide. Through the gap, without touching the shutters, you can see the back of the house.

It's better than you expected, though it isn't perfect. Your room is on the corner. Below and to the right is the yard: wet cobbles, a stack of empty barrels, a covered well and a handcart tipped on its end. Across the yard stands the wall, head-high, with the gate in it, a plank door with an iron ring latch. A lamp hangs unlit on a hook beside it, and an alley lane runs past outside. From up here you'd see anyone who comes through that gate, and every step they take on the stones.

You wouldn't see the back door. It sits right below you, under the slope of a lean-to roof over the kitchen, and the tiles cut off everything past the middle of the yard. You'd see someone cross the yard and then lose them under the eaves.

With the candle unlit, the room behind you is black. From the yard, the broken slat would be just another dark gap in an old shutter.

The cat jumps onto the end of the bed, walks the length of the blanket, and then goes to the sill. It sits upright beside the shutter with its nose at the gap, looking down into the yard as if it had read your mind. Down the bond comes something small and dry. It isn't worry. It's closer to *this is better than the chair*.

*Much better. No sitting in strange chairs tonight.*

I leave the candle unlit and settle beside the window, far enough back that my face won’t show through the gap. My cloak stays on; the rod rests within reach.

I keep watch over the yard and listen for the gate latch, waiting to see who comes to meet Dorrin after closing.
turns.reply:
The candle stays dark. You set your back against the wall beside the window, far enough back that the gap in the slat is only a thin grey line against your eye, and lay the rod across your knee. The cat stays on the sill, a black shape against a darker one.

The house goes on without you. Through the floorboards the taproom winds down slowly. A song starts and dies. Hesta calls last orders loud enough to rattle the jug on the washstand, and benches scrape. The front door opens and shuts again and again, and the voices in the street get fewer and drunker and further off. Somewhere near midnight the heavy bolt of the front door goes home with a sound you feel in the floor more than hear.

Soon after, light quick steps come up a back stair at the far end of the passage, a door closes, and a bar drops. That's Ilsa. Hesta's heavier tread follows a while later. Downstairs one voice is still talking now and then, low and pleasant, to nobody. Cards whisper on felt. Dorrin is dealing to an empty room.

The yard stays black and wet. Twice a rat crosses the cobbles by the barrels, and twice the cat's ears follow it and lose interest. The cold works in under the shutters. A bell somewhere up the hill tolls one.

Then the ring latch on the yard gate lifts.

It's slow and careful, iron easing against iron. The gate swings in just wide enough for one man. You lean a hair closer to the slat, and on the sill the cat goes utterly still.

A man comes through. That's all you can make of him. It's a shape darker than the dark, cloaked to the heels and hooded, a little taller than the gate's iron ring. He doesn't carry a light. He doesn't look up. He pulls the gate to behind him without letting the latch drop, so it can't clack.

Then his heels cross the cobbles. Ilsa was right about them: *click, click*, hard and unhurried, the walk of a man who wants the stones to know he's there. He passes the well and the tipped handcart, and at the middle of the yard the lean-to's tiles cut him off. You hear the back door open beneath you. It doesn't creak. Someone keeps its hinges oiled.

You strain after the rest and get nothing. Two voices murmur somewhere under your floor, one of them warm and easy, the other flat and low. You can't pick out a single word through the boards. You can't tell how tall he is, or what he wears under that cloak, or whether he came down from the hill or only walks as if he did. You didn't see his face at all. The night is too dark and he's too careful, and for all your watching you've caught no more than Ilsa did.

The talk goes on longer than you'd like. Once the warm voice laughs, short. Once the flat one says something, and a pause follows, long enough that you notice it.

Then the back door again. The heels come out from under the eaves and go back the way they came, at the same pace, past the cart and the well. The gate opens a man's width. He's through, and the latch is eased down so softly you only know it's closed because the gap is gone. The heels go away down the alley and fade into the ordinary noises of the city at night: a dog, a cart somewhere, water dripping off the eaves.

The cat stays at the slat a while longer, ears forward, watching the empty gate. Then it turns its head and looks at you in the dark. It doesn't send anything down the bond. Below, faintly, cards whisper on felt again.

 You didn't see enough. However hard you watched, the dark yard and the hood kept the visitor's face, his clothes and his business from you. Through the floor you heard two voices but not one word, and your watch ended with no more than Ilsa had already told you: someone in hard heels comes in by the gate and goes out the same way.

turns.message:
*We tried,* I tell the cat. *Morning, then.*

I leave the door barred, put the rod beside the bed, and take off my armour. Before lying down, I hold Tymora’s coin for a moment.

“If you sent me for him, Lady, I’ve found him. I’ll do what I can.”

I get some sleep until Hesta knocks for the locksmith.
turns.reply:
*We tried.* The cat stays on the sill a moment longer. Then it jumps down without a sound, as if it has decided the yard isn't worth any more of its time, and walks the length of the bed to the pillow end. It turns round twice there.

You leave the bar across the door and lean the rod against the bedframe, where your hand will find it in the dark. The studded leather comes off in stages: buckles, then laces stiff with the cold. You lay it over the washstand. Without it the room feels colder.

The coin is still cool when you take it out from under your shirt. It isn't the cold it had in the taproom, only the ordinary chill of metal at night. You close your hand round it and say your piece quietly to the dark room.

Nothing answers in words. After a few breaths the coin warms in your fist the way coins always do when you hold them, and you can't honestly say whether it's more than that. Then you lie down. The cat settles into the crook behind your knees. It's a solid, warm weight there, and it doesn't move again.

You sleep.

At some point you dream. It isn't much of a dream. There's green felt under a lamp, and a coin spinning on it, bright and fast. You wait for it to slow down and fall, the way they always do. It slows. It wobbles. Then it stops upright on its rim, perfectly still, and doesn't fall either way. Something small sits across the table from you in the dark, past the lamplight. It doesn't reach for the coin. You get the feeling it's waiting to see what you'll do. Then the dream goes the way dreams go, and you're left with only the shape of it: a coin that wouldn't land.

Once you half wake. Down below, the heavy front bolt slides back, there's a pause, and then it goes home again. The cat's ear twitches against your leg. Somebody has been let out into the street. You're asleep again before you can think about who.

The next thing you know is the knock.

Hesta warned you she knocks loud, and she meant it. Three blows land on the door like someone driving a peg into a beam, and the jug on the washstand rattles. Grey light shows at the broken slat. It's thin and early, and somewhere down towards the harbour a gull is complaining about it. The room smells of cold tallow and lye. The cat is already sitting up on the blanket with its eyes on the door.

"Worgen." Hesta's voice comes through the planks without any trouble. "Marl's downstairs. He's got his bag, he's in a mood, and the box is on my bar." A pause. "Our friend went home three hours since. The room's empty. You'll want your boots on."

Her footsteps go away down the passage, heavy and unhurried, then down the stair.

Your armour is still over the washstand where you left it.

(Out of game: you slept a little under five hours, which isn't enough for a long rest. You hadn't used any spells or hit dice, so you lose nothing by it.)

turns.message:
“Coming.”

I wash my face, buckle on my armour and gather my gear, then head downstairs with the cat.

“Master Tenby? James Worgen. Thank you for coming early.” I nod toward the box. “We’d like the lock opened without damage, if possible. What’s your fee?”
turns.reply:
Cold water from the cracked jug takes the last of the sleep off your face. The studded leather goes back on in the grey light, laces first, then buckles, and it sits stiff and chilly until your body warms it. Rod, coin, pack. The cat is already at the door when you lift the bar, and it goes down the stair ahead of you this time.

The taproom looks different empty. The benches are stacked and the hearth is banked to a dull red eye. There's a smell of cold ash, and the floor has been swept so recently the boards are still damp. Grey dawn comes in through the front shutters in thin bars. In the far corner the card table is bare felt under the unlit lantern. The little tower of coins still sits in front of the empty chair. Nobody has touched it.

The box sits on the bar between Hesta's two fists. Ilsa stands at the end of the counter with her shawl still on, cheeks pink from the run downhill and the morning cold. Her eyes go to the corner and come straight back.

The man beside the box has to be Marl Tenby. He's thin and stooped, somewhere past sixty, with a bald head, a fringe of white hair and a leather apron worn shiny at the belly. A canvas roll lies open on the bar beside him: hooks, rakes, tension wires, a tiny oil can, all laid out in a neat row. He doesn't look up when you come down. He's peering into the keyhole with a jeweller's glass screwed into one eye.

At your greeting he takes the glass out and looks at you the way he looked at the lock.

"Two gold. One for the lock, one for the hour." His voice is dry and quiet, and he doesn't waste any of it. "After. If it opens clean. If it doesn't, nothing." He taps one fingernail on the scratched wood round the keyhole. "Someone's been at this with a knife. Wrong tool, wrong hand. Didn't get past the plate."

He doesn't wait for an answer. He oils the keyhole with one drop, slides in a bent wire, then a second, finer one, and goes still with his head tilted, listening to something only he can hear. Hesta holds her breath. You can tell because she stops filling the room. The cat jumps up onto the stool beside you and sits with its tail wrapped round its feet, watching his hands.

It doesn't take long. Marl's wrist turns a hair's breadth, then another. There's a small, solid *click*, the kind a lock makes when it's done arguing.

Marl draws his wires out, wipes them on his apron and lays them back in their places in the roll. Then he lifts the lid with one finger, steps back half a pace, and looks at the ceiling. He's a man who opens other people's secrets for a living and has trained himself not to read them.

The lid creaks up on stiff hinges.

There's no silver.

The inside is lined with faded green baize, the colour of a card table's felt. Two things lie on it.

The first is a letter. It's folded small and thick, several sheets, and sealed with a blob of plain brown wax. Pressed into the wax is the mark you've seen twice now: a circle the size of a fingernail with a short notch in its rim. Across the outside, in a small, quick, slanting hand, someone has written:

*To the next one she sends.*

The ink is as dark as the day it was written. Nothing on it has worn away.

The second thing is a scrap of stiff yellowed card with a torn edge, a pawnbroker's ticket. It's printed in smudged black, with blanks filled in by hand:

**GRISWELL'S — LENDING & SURETY**
*The Undercellar, foot of the Wet Stair*
**No. 4471**
*Article:* coin, gold, old strike, 1
*Advanced:* 1 sp
*Pledged by:*

The space after *Pledged by* is smooth and blank, exactly like the tag on the box.

Hesta looks at the ticket for a long moment, then at the empty baize where her three months should have been. She breathes out through her nose.

"One silver," she says. "He pawned it for one silver. His coin. The one he flipped for everything." She shakes her head slowly. She isn't angry. She looks like a woman finally getting the end of a joke she was told years ago. "That little devil. Never paid me in anything but jokes, and this is the last one."

Ilsa has come a step closer down the bar without seeming to notice. She's looking at the letter and the words on it, and she doesn't ask what they mean.

On the stool, the cat leans forward and puts its nose almost to the wax seal. It doesn't send you anything down the bond. Its whiskers go forward, and it stays like that.

Over in the corner, at seat-back height above the empty chair, the cold dawn air does nothing at all. You have the feeling, the one you get at a table when the whole room is waiting on one card, that somebody is holding very still.

Marl Tenby is still studying the ceiling. He clears his throat once, quietly, the way a man reminds you he's owed two gold without saying so.

turns.message:
I count two gold pieces onto the bar beside Marl’s tools. “Cleanly done. Thank you.”

Then I pick up the letter. “I believe this one’s meant for me.”

I carefully break the wax seal, unfold the sheets and read.
turns.reply:
Marl Tenby doesn't count the two gold pieces. He watches them land on the bar, slides them into his apron with one finger and nods once. He seems to have no more use for words than he has for gossip.

"Clean lock," he says. "Good morning."

He rolls his canvas shut, ties it with a single turn of string and goes out without looking at the box again. The front door lets in a gust of harbour air, gulls and wet stone, and then it shuts behind him.

The letter is lighter than it looks. The brown wax gives under your thumb with a dry little crack, and the notched circle breaks clean down the middle. Four sheets are folded inside, small and thick. They're written edge to edge in the same quick, slanting hand, as if the writer was trying to get it all down before his candle burned out.

*To the next one she sends.*

*If you're reading this, two things are true. She sent you, and I lost. I'm sorry about the second one. I did try.*

*My name is*

Your eyes stop there. Something should come after those words, and nothing does. It isn't a gap or a blot. Your eye slides across that bit of paper the way a boot slides on ice, and lands on the next line before you've decided to move it.

*There, I expect you've noticed something wrong with that line. If I've guessed right about what they do to a man, you can't read it and the good woman downstairs can't remember it. Tell her the jokes were free and the rent wasn't, and I know it.*

*The Lady sent me here when the city was still full of smoke and refugees. I'd bet my boots it was on the same terms as you. I found what I was sent for. A patriar on the hill, Lord Esmond Ardanne, has been buying fair winds for his ships, and he isn't buying them from Umberlee. There's a paper. I've seen the bottom of it. The name signed there doesn't belong to anybody who was in the room.*

*I couldn't get at the paper, so he offered me a way. One game at a table of his choosing, me against his luck. If I win, the paper burns. If I lose, I'm staked. He was very polite about what that means. The dealer is a sharp called Vasque. He isn't a good one, and that's the only reason I said yes.*

*Then a clerk with black under his nails took my coin, her coin, the one the Hall gave me, and scraped her face off the back of it to seal the wager. It won't land since then. Not heads, not tails. It stands up on its edge and looks at me. I've flipped it a hundred times tonight.*

*So I've put it where neither they nor I can easily get at it. The ticket's in with this. If I win, I'll fetch it back myself for a silver and you'll never read a word of this. If you are reading it, go and get it before they think to. And don't throw it until you know which side you want it to land on. I don't know. That's the truth, and it's why I haven't thrown it.*

*Three things, and then I'll stop being serious, because it doesn't suit me.*

*Don't sit in any chair at a table they're running.*

*Don't touch whatever's piled in front of it, however it looks.*

*Don't let anybody wager you. Not for you, not against you, not even as a joke.*

*I told the Hall. The Hall told me to be patient. Don't go to them first.*

*Good luck. I mean that professionally.*

There's a dash at the bottom, and after it the same smooth nothing your eyes won't hold. Under that, drawn by hand in the ink, is the circle with the notch in its rim.

As you read the three warnings, the coin under your collar cools. It isn't the winter-windowsill cold from last night, only a faint chill, like a draught from a door left ajar. It's gone by the time you turn the last sheet.

Hesta hasn't moved. She stands with both fists on the bar and watches your face the way she watched the ticket. She can't see the words from where she stands, and she doesn't lean over to try. Down at the end of the counter, Ilsa holds her shawl closed at her throat with one hand. She looks at the letter, then at the corner, and this time her eyes don't come straight back.

The cat has taken its nose off the broken seal. It sits upright on the stool, tail round its feet, and looks across the empty taproom at the chair. Then it looks at you. Down the bond comes a single, firm, warm feeling, the one it gives when the door's barred and the rod is by the bed. It means *yes. That's him.*

The pawn ticket still lies on the green baize. Grey light shows on the smudged print: *the Undercellar, foot of the Wet Stair.*

“He says the jokes were free and the rent wasn’t. He knew he owed you.” I pause. “I believe he’s still in that chair. And I have a lead on helping him.”

The letter goes inside your coat, against your shirt, beside the Lady's coin. Hesta watches it go.

When you give her his message, she doesn't say anything at first. Her mouth works once, as if she's chewing something tough. Then a short laugh comes out through her nose. There isn't much humour in it, but there's a lot of something else.

"He knew. Course he knew." She wipes the heel of her hand across one eye, quickly, the way someone brushes off flour. "Twelve weeks he stood at this bar and told me he'd pay Tuesday."

Then you tell her he's still in the chair.

She goes still. She doesn't argue. For the first time since you walked in last night, Hesta Morrow turns her head and looks straight at the corner. She looks at the bare felt, the unlit lantern, the little tower of coins in front of the empty chair. She keeps looking for a long moment.

"Five winters," she says quietly. That's all.

You lower your voice and give them his three warnings, word for word: don't sit, don't touch the pile, don't let anyone wager you. Hesta listens with her jaw set. At the end of the bar Ilsa holds her shawl tight and moves her lips along with the words, as if she's learning a house rule.

"I clear that table every night," Ilsa says when you've finished. "I've never touched the pile. I wipe round it." She hesitates. "I'll go on wiping round it."

"Nobody tells Dorrin anything in my house he didn't bring in himself," Hesta says. "He pays his corner rent. That's all he gets from me." She looks at the pawn ticket in your hand and doesn't reach for it. "That's his. You're taking it to him, near enough. Go on."

Then she thinks about your question, and her face turns practical again.

"Safest way's to go now. The Undercellar sleeps late, same as the folk who use it. Go down Cable Street past Marl's and keep on to the fish market on the harbour. Behind the gutting tables there's an old brick arch. The Wet Stair goes down under it. They sluice the market out every morning and it all runs down those steps, so mind your feet. It's not called wet for nothing." She holds up a finger. "There'll be a boy at the top with a lamp. He'll ask you for a copper for the light. Pay it and don't argue. It's not his copper, it's the Guild's, and they remember who didn't pay."

A second finger.

"Wear your blade, but leave it alone, and keep that stick of yours out of your hand. Down there a man who looks ready for trouble gets offered some." She glances at the cat. "And keep him close. They'll have the whiskers off him for luck."

The cat gives her a long, flat look from the stool.

"Old Griswell lends to sailors against their boots and their wedding rings. Last I heard he was alive and mean with it." Her frown comes back. "But five winters is a long time to hold a pledge worth one silver. I'd have sold it in one. Either he's soft, which he isn't, or somebody's asked him not to."

Out on the street a cart rattles past. Somewhere down towards the harbour a bell rings for the fish market opening. Ilsa glances at the front door, then at the hatch. The breakfast crowd will be coming soon.

"Go on, then." Hesta has already turned to the box. She closes the empty lid on its green baize and sets it back under the bar where it has sat for five winters. "Mind the steps. I'm not having you carried back up my stair on a door."

Ilsa doesn't say anything. As you go she gives you a small nod, the kind a server gives a regular, and then the kitchen hatch bangs and she's gone into the smell of porridge.

The rod goes into its loop under your cloak. You put the ticket inside your coat, in the same pocket as the letter, and button the flap over it. At *close by me* the cat drops off the stool and takes up a place at your left heel. It stays there out of the door and into the street.

Cable Street wakes up around you as you go downhill. The cobbles are wet from a night's drizzle and shine grey in the dawn. Marl Tenby's shutters are open now, and through the window you can see him bent over a workbench with the jeweller's glass already back in his eye. He doesn't look up. Past his shop the ropewalk runs a long way under a lean-to roof. Two men walk backwards down it, twisting hemp, with the slow care of people who have done the same thing for twenty years. The air smells of tar and wet rope, and by the bottom of the street it smells of fish as well.

The fish market sprawls along the harbour wall, under a sky full of gulls. The boats came in an hour ago. Long trestle tables run in rows, and women in leather aprons stand at them gutting with short knives, so fast their hands blur. Scales fly. The gulls fight over the slops in the gutters, and one of them makes a pass at the cat. The cat turns its head and looks at it, and the gull decides it wanted something else.

At the end of the row a crier stands on an upturned crate with a bundle of broadsheets under his arm. He calls in the flat, practised bawl of a man who has been doing it since the bells.

"*Baldur's Mouth*, one copper! Fist says the Outer City curfew stands another tenday! Grain barge aground at Wyrm's Crossing! Another one in the water off the Grey Harbour steps last night, coin in his teeth like the others, and the Fist says *no foul play*! One copper, *Baldur's Mouth*!"

The nearest fishwife stops gutting just long enough to touch two wet fingers to her lips and then to the table's edge. It's a sailor's sign for Umberlee, done without thinking. Her neighbour doesn't make the sign. She spits in the gutter instead and goes back to her knife.

Behind the last row of tables, where the market backs onto an old warehouse wall, is the arch. It's a low curve of soot-black brick, older than the warehouse it's built into, and its keystone has been worn shapeless by weather. Two lads are sluicing out the market with buckets and a long-handled broom, and the dirty water runs over the cobbles straight under the arch and down. You hear it before you see the stair. It gurgles and slaps, a long way down, like water going into a well.

The steps go down steep and narrow into the dark, slick with fish slime and green weed. The first dozen are lit grey by the morning. After that there's nothing.

On the top step, with his back against the brick and out of the stream of water, sits a boy of ten or eleven. He has a shuttered tin lamp between his bare feet and a cap pulled down to his eyebrows. His feet are filthy. His eyes are sharp. He has seen your boots, your cloak and the way you carry yourself before you're halfway across the cobbles, and by the time you reach the arch he's on his feet with the lamp in one hand and the other held out, palm up.

"Copper for the light, mister." He says it the way the crier says *one copper*, like a fixed price. His eyes drop to the cat at your heel and come back up. "Cat goes free. Cats see in the dark."

Down below, the water goes on slapping at something you can't see.

(Out of game: your purse holds only gold pieces, 347 of them, with no silver or copper.)

turns.reply:
The boy looks at you standing on the level cobbles. Then he looks down at the slick top step, where the market water runs past his heels, and seems to decide that you have more sense than most of the men he sees.

"Change a *gold*?" He snorts, not unkindly. "Mister, if I had change for gold I wouldn't be sat on a wet step." He tips his head at the end of the row, where the crier is still bawling from his crate. "Old Tam. He's been selling the Mouth since the bells, so his bag's all coppers. Buy a sheet off him and he'll break your gold, but he'll moan about it." He thinks for a moment. "Or the fishwives. They'll break it too, but they'll want you to buy a fish."

He sits back down against the brick with the lamp between his feet. He doesn't call after you or try to talk you round. Sharp eyes follow your hand to your purse and away again, the way a man counts cards he isn't meant to see.

"I'll be here," he says. "Nobody goes down without the light." He nods at the cat. "Except him."

The cat sits at your heel on the wet cobbles. It looks at the boy, then at the dark stair, and its tail curls tight round its feet. It doesn't send you anything down the bond, but it hasn't put a paw near the first step either.

Behind you, Tam's voice carries over the gulls: "*Baldur's Mouth*, one copper! Coin in his teeth, and the Fist says no foul play!"

note.text:
I enjoyed this session. James had room to be a person before he had a quest: refusing cards, talking to an innkeeper, worrying about his cat, paying for supper. The mystery grew naturally out of those choices.

**What worked**
- Hesta, Ilsa and the cat were the strongest parts. They had distinct personalities, and small gestures made earning their trust satisfying.
- The hook fit James unusually well. The missing name, abandoned stake and trapped servant of Tymora made this personal without forcing me to sit down and gamble.
- My refusals mattered. Dorrin tempted me, but the game let me investigate another way.
- The clues were memorable and consistent: the notched coin, erased names, cold chair and coin that wouldn’t land. The letter delivered a useful payoff.
- Failed checks stayed failed, even after a reroll. I appreciated that honesty.

**What broke**
- The rules and records weren’t fully aligned. Arcana used +2 instead of +3; the failed Perception reroll was later logged as the original result. The initial record also changed some supplied character details without explanation, including rapier proficiency, Healing Light’s limit and attunement.
- Out-of-game notes sometimes explained things nobody had disputed. One referenced “the fourth item” and a “misreading” with no visible context. That felt like internal bookkeeping leaking into the scene.
- The narration occasionally treated mood as evidence—for example, James sensing Dorrin watching his back. I’d prefer observable details or clearly labelled suspicions.

**What was missing / could improve**
- More momentum. We spent most of a session on one tavern conversation and reached the next location just as play ended. The atmosphere was good, but repeated looks, pauses, rag-wiping and cat reactions sometimes slowed it down.
- Routine logistics could be bundled. Getting change for a one-copper toll became several turns without presenting much of a meaningful choice.
- Checks required a roll request, a button press and sometimes an additional “Onward.” Resolving the narration immediately after the roll would help.
- A little more ordinary city life alongside the mystery would make the setting feel less arranged around it. The fish market and broadsheet were welcome.

Overall, I’d gladly continue. Keep the characterful NPCs and respect for player choice; tighten the repetition, streamline routine actions and make the mechanical records dependable.

opening.text: The Basilisk Gate is behind you, and the city closes around you the way big ports do: noise, lamplight, too many people with somewhere to be. The Copper Lantern is the first door that promised warmth, and it keeps its promise. Heat from the hearth, the roar of a full taproom, the smell of fried fish and wet wool. A broad woman behind the bar is chalking names onto a slate of rooms while she pours. A young tiefling with a tray slides between benches, and more than one drinker leans away from her as she passes. In the far corner, under a swinging lantern, cards snap onto felt. The dealer has quick hands and an easy smile, and the players are hunched over their hands with the stillness of people who have money on the table. One seat there is empty. In front of it sits a small, tidy tower of coins that nobody reaches for and nobody seems to notice. The cat has stopped dead at your boots. Tail low, it stares at that empty chair and will not look away. The innkeeper glances up from her slate and catches your eye across the room. She raises her brows: a bed, a drink, or just the door letting in the cold?
